questions.question: A baby is born with a few instincts, behaviours that need no teaching at all. Which of these can a baby do on the day she is born?
questions.answer: Grip a finger placed in her palm
choices: Grip a finger placed in her palm
Reach out to grab a toy
Wave bye-bye to her family
Lift her arms to be picked up
questions.context: A newborn's fingers curl tight round anything pressed into her palm, a reflex she is born with that fades by about six months. Reaching for a toy, lifting her arms to be picked up and waving bye-bye all come many months later, as she grows and learns from the people around her.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.13B has 5th graders tell instinctive from learned behaviour, and a newborn's grasp shows that people are born with instincts too.

questions.question: A young garden spider spins a web, a wheel of silk threads for catching flies. How did it come to know how to build it?
choices: It was born knowing how
Its mother taught it how
It watched older spiders at work
It copied a web it found nearby
questions.context: Web spinning is an instinct: young spiders build working webs without ever watching one being made or being taught. A garden spider's mother dies in late autumn, soon after laying her eggs, and the young hatch the next spring and scatter to build webs of their own.
questions.grade_note: A spider spinning its web is a standard 5th-grade example of an instinct, the inborn half of TEKS 5.13B.

questions.question: Sea-turtle hatchlings dig out of their sandy nest, usually at night, and crawl straight down the beach to the sea. They are born knowing the way. Why does a hatchling need to know it from birth?
questions.answer: Its mother left long before it hatched
choices: Its mother left long before it hatched
Its mother is busy guarding the other eggs
Its mother waits to teach it out at sea
Its mother can lead only a few at a time
questions.context: A mother sea turtle lays her eggs at night, covers them with sand and goes back to the sea, and the eggs hatch about two months later in a nest no adult watches over. With no one to show them, the hatchlings find the sea by instinct, crawling toward the brightest part of the sky, which on a dark beach lies over the water.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.13B names turtle hatchlings returning to the sea as its example of an instinct that raises the chance of survival, and the reason it matters is that no adult is there to teach them.

questions.question: People are born with some behaviours that keep them safe, and they learn others as they grow up. Which of these safe behaviours has to be learned?
questions.answer: Looking both ways before crossing a road
choices: Looking both ways before crossing a road
Sneezing when dust tickles the nose
Coughing when a crumb sticks in the throat
Jerking back a hand that touches a hot pan
questions.context: Children are taught to look both ways, and then again, before they cross a street. Sneezing, coughing and snatching a hand back from heat are reflexes: the body does them by itself, with no lessons, to protect itself.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.13B asks how both inborn and learned behaviours help survival, and sorting a person's reflexes from taught safety habits is part of it.

questions.question: A pet dog sits, lies down or lifts a paw to shake whenever its owner asks. How does a dog usually come to do a trick like this?
questions.answer: It is rewarded each time it does it
choices: It is rewarded each time it does it
It is born with an instinct for it
It practises the trick on its own
It simply grows into it with age
questions.context: Tricks are learned: the owner gives the dog a treat or praise each time it does the trick, and soon it does the trick on command. A trained dog's puppies are not born knowing its tricks, because a learned behaviour is not inherited: each puppy has to learn the trick for itself.
questions.grade_note: Texas's grade 5 standard named an animal learning tricks as its example of a learned behaviour (TEKS 112.16(b)(10)(B)), and the 2021 standard 5.13B keeps learned behaviour.

questions.question: Milk was once left on British doorsteps in glass bottles with thin foil caps. Small birds called blue tits began pecking through the caps to drink the cream at the top, and the habit spread from town to town. How does being able to learn like this help animals survive?
questions.answer: They can change their ways as things change
choices: They can change their ways as things change
They can act right the very first time they try
They can pass new skills on through their eggs
They can get by without any instincts
questions.context: No instinct could have prepared a bird for a milk bottle, but learning let blue tits make use of a brand-new source of food. Instincts stay the same, while learned behaviours can change to fit a changing world, and a new skill is not passed on in an egg: each young bird must learn it.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.13B asks how learned behaviours increase the chance of survival, and fitting behaviour to new conditions is the main reason taught.

questions.question: Ana was adopted as a newborn and grew up in another country, far from her birth parents. Which of her traits came to her from her birth parents?
choices: The colour of her eyes
The language she speaks
Her skill at the piano
The scar on her knee
questions.context: Eye colour is inherited: it is set by genes passed down from parents. The language Ana speaks, her piano playing and her scar all came from her own life, from the family that raised her, her practice and an old fall.
questions.grade_note: 5th graders learn to tell inherited traits from things gained in life (TEKS 112.16(b)(10)(B); NGSS LS3.A), with eye colour against a scar or a skill as the classic pair.

ad7c7c7379.why: Judge (low): 'its first web' claimed the very first web is already wheel-shaped (F6's caveat: spiderlings raised alone first lay shapeless silk) and hinted there was no practice; the stem now says 'spins a web'. Judge (low): 'It learned from its brothers and sisters' was the weakest lure (and partly arguable, since spiderlings cluster for a week after hatching); 'It copied a web it found nearby' replaces it, another learning route a child might believe, false by F6 (webs are built without observation). Key and context unchanged.

d13dab9ea2.why: Judge (high): the stem called the crawl an instinct, which ruled out both learning lures, and the key restated the definition of an instinct. The question now keys the survival reason the judge named (F9, F25): the mother covers the nest and goes back to the sea about two months before the eggs hatch, so no adult is there to teach. Every choice is a claim about the mother, and the three lures each put her on hand (guarding the nest, teaching at sea, leading a few), the young-learn-from-mother idea (M2), all false by F9 and F25 (no parental care). The stem keeps 'born knowing the way' as the premise; it rules out no choice. The spider still keys 'it is inborn'; the turtle keys why that matters.

5707d900a7.why: Fact-check (uncertain): 'look left, right and left again' is the right-hand-traffic drill; Britain's drill runs the other way (F26). The context now says 'look both ways, and then again'. Judge (low): 'Jerking a hand back from a hot pan' could be read as the learned lesson after a burn; it is now 'Jerking back a hand that touches a hot pan', plainly the withdrawal reflex (F14). Stem and key unchanged.

4d7ce512e6.why: Fact-check (error): the context said 'a learned behaviour is not passed on to the young', which is false (learned behaviour spreads by teaching and copying, as the blue tits show); it now says a learned behaviour is not inherited: each puppy has to learn the trick for itself (F20, F29). Judge (medium): 'It is born with an instinct for it' and 'It inherits the trick from its parents' both meant 'inborn' and fell together. The inheritance lure is replaced by 'It practises the trick on its own', a second learning route a child might believe (people practise skills alone), false because tricks come from the owner's rewards (F13). The judge's 'learns it from its mother as a puppy' was not used: the fact-check's own source shows puppies can learn by watching their mother, so it would be partly true. Stem and key unchanged.

fd8d06002c.why: Judge (low, cheap clarity fixes): the stem now says the blue tits are small birds, which a US 5th grader may not know, and that the cream sat at the top of the bottle (F28). No date was added (the 1921 first record was of waxboard tops). Key, choices and context unchanged.

61b71e1584.why: Judge (low): the key 'Her brown eyes' was the shortest choice; it is now 'The colour of her eyes', the same fact (F19). Judge (low): 'Her skill at swimming' echoed adaptations-built-for-a-place's duckling lure; it is now 'Her skill at the piano', still a skill gained in life (F20). The context follows. Stem unchanged.

added.90ea79e4bf: Replaces the dropped blacksmith with the learned-behaviour question the scope names and the unit lacked: a child riding a bicycle (F24, TEKS 112.16(b)(10)(B)). It keys that a practised, automatic skill is still learned (F27, F1), the confusion of an automatic skill with an instinct (M3); the stem's 'as easily as he breathes' pulls toward the instinct lure. Each lure is a distinct false claim, so none falls with another: practice turns it into an instinct (false, F1), his children will be born able to ride (false, F20, M1), a month off would lose it (false, F27). A general human skill, no species' behaviour. Facts F1, F20, F24, F27.

dropped.question: A blacksmith swings a heavy hammer every day for twenty years, and his arms grow thick with muscle. Will his baby son be born with arms like his?
dropped.why: Judge said drop, and I agree: common sense answers it (no baby is born with a blacksmith's muscled arms), 'No, a son inherits only from his mother' is plainly wrong and 'Yes, if the work came before the boy's birth' confused; and its fact (a change gained in life is not inherited) is already keyed by Ana's question here and keyed again by mendels-peas-and-inherited-traits' own blacksmith question.

dropped.question: A man has ridden a bicycle to work every day for twenty years. Now he rides without a thought, as easily as he breathes. Which of these is true of his riding?
dropped.why: failed the re-check: Facts hold (riding is procedural memory, practised, lasting; not inborn, not inherited), but the key is a standout: only it answers the stem's set-up ('however easy it feels' echoes 'as easily as he breathes'), with the corrective 'still', and it is the longest choice. Two lures fall to everyday knowledge (every child learned to ride, so no baby is born able to, the blacksmith's flaw; 'you never forget how to ride a bike'), leaving only the instinct lure live.
